areas.n: Wheeling, WV (downtown, Centre Market, Oglebay, Wheeling Island)
Ohio Valley — St. Clairsville & Belmont County OH
Cambridge & Guernsey County (Dickens Village, Salt Fork)
Zanesville & the National Road to the Columbus edge (Muskingum, New Concord, Norwich)

P.ad: 1010 Main St over the Ohio River (US-40), Wheeling, WV 26003
P.w: The oldest major long-span suspension bridge in the world still carrying traffic. Built by Charles Ellet Jr. in 1849 (1010 ft, then the world's longest); rebuilt 1856 after a tornado, stay cables later added to a Washington Roebling design. NRHP 1970, ASCE National Historic Civil Engineering Landmark, National Historic Landmark 1976.

The birthplace of West Virginia and a National Historic Landmark. Built 1859-60 as a federal custom house; site of the Wheeling Conventions and first WV Constitutional Convention that made the state during the Civil War. Restored museum, free tours Tue-Sat.

1,700-acre municipal resort on industrialist Earl Oglebay's former estate. Home to the Good Zoo (WV's only AZA-accredited zoo), the Carriage House Glass Museum (3,000+ pieces of Wheeling glass incl. the 5-ft Sweeney Punch Bowl), the Mansion Museum, gardens, golf, and the winter Festival of Lights (300+ acres, 1M+ lights).

Historic market district anchored by the 1853 Centre Market house, the oldest cast-iron market house in the country (older than the state itself). Two market buildings plus a walkable block of antique shops, eateries and salons; monthly First Friday events. NRHP historic district.
Restored 1928 downtown theatre and full entertainment complex; home of the Wheeling Symphony Orchestra and host to touring Broadway, comedy and concert acts (Jerry Seinfeld, Willie Nelson).
Tens of thousands of toys and trains housed in a restored 1906 Victorian schoolhouse, with a 2,000+ sq ft operating model-train layout, rotating exhibits and guided tours. A family favorite.

P.ad: Riverfront trailheads along the Ohio River, Wheeling, WV 26003
P.w: About 13.5 miles of paved rail-trail on former railroad beds, looping through the city and along the Ohio River for walking and cycling.

P.n: Oglebay Institute's Stifel Fine Arts Center
P.w: "Edemar," a 1910-14 Classical Revival mansion given to the Oglebay Institute in 1976 and run as an arts center with galleries, exhibitions and classes. Listed on the National Register of Historic Places (1992).

P.ad: 91 Kruger St, Elm Grove, Wheeling, WV 26003
P.w: Stone plantation house built 1798 by Moses Shepherd on the old National Road, later renamed Monument Place. NRHP-listed. Owned by the Osiris Shrine Temple; interior access is limited (events/appointment) rather than a regular public museum.

P.ad: Wheeling Island (across the Suspension Bridge), Wheeling, WV 26003
P.w: A large residential island in the Ohio River with 1,110+ contributing buildings in Italianate, Queen Anne and Craftsman styles; NRHP historic district (1992). Also home to the Wheeling Island racetrack and casino.

A National Historic Landmark rock overhang holding evidence of human habitation ~16,000-19,000 years ago — the oldest known site of human habitation in North America. Operated by the Heinz History Center; interpretive villages (16th-c. Indian village, 18th-c. trading post, 19th-c. village). Seasonal (roughly May-Oct).

1812 home of abolitionist Dr. F. Julius LeMoyne — Pennsylvania's first National Historic Landmark of the Underground Railroad. LeMoyne also built the Western Hemisphere's first crematory (tourable). Run by the Washington County Historical Society.

A ~4-mile scenic round-trip aboard restored streetcars from a collection of nearly 50 cars (PA, WV, OH and beyond), plus a Visitor Education Center with a trolley simulator, exhibits and film. A top family stop.
1788 stone townhouse of David Bradford, a leader of the 1794 Whiskey Rebellion. Restored house museum with period furnishings, hand-embroidered wainscot (1773) and a children's room.

A 1900 Beaux-Arts courthouse by architect Frederick J. Osterling, crowned by a 150-ft dome topped with a statue of George Washington, with a grand central stairway and 40-ft stained-glass ceiling. NRHP 1974; still in use.

A monumental sandstone railroad viaduct (1871) with 43 stone arches — the 37 ring stones symbolize the 37 states of the reunited Union. Built by the B&O/Central Ohio Railroads as the "Great Shortline to the West." NRHP 1976; walking trail opened to the public 2022.

Built 1828, the oldest bridge in Ohio and the longest (345 ft) surviving three-arch sandstone "S" bridge on the National Road — the first federally funded highway. Named Ohio's official Bicentennial Bridge in 2003.

A 26-room Romanesque Revival mansion (1888-93, the Bradfield house), formerly the "Gay '90s" museum, filled with period decoration. Open year-round by appointment; especially popular as a holiday destination.

The largest remaining old-growth forest tract in southeastern Ohio — a 50-acre core of 300-400-year-old oaks (some over 4 ft around) within a 455-acre preserve, the only known remnant mixed-mesophytic forest in Ohio. Hiking trails; part of the Old-Growth Forest Network.

Each holiday season downtown Cambridge is transformed into a Dickens-era streetscape of life-size Victorian character scenes, capped by the Guernsey County Courthouse light-and-music show (85,000+ lights). Seasonal: Nov 1 - Jan 1.
Ohio's largest state park — 17,229 acres of land and 2,952 of water, with a lodge, an 18-hole golf course, a 2,500-ft swimming beach, marinas, a nature center and extensive hiking/equestrian trails.

A working handcrafted-pressed-glass factory (40+ years) offering weekday factory-floor tours where you watch artisans press glass, plus a showroom. Factory tours Mon-Fri (morning/early-afternoon windows); showroom Mon-Fri.

Home of the National Cambridge Collectors, with 10,000+ pieces of the world-famous Cambridge Glass Company's elegant glassware and interactive exhibits. Seasonal: Apr-Oct (Wed-Sun), limited winter hours.

Cambridge was the birthplace of William Boyd, the actor who played cowboy hero Hopalong Cassidy. A downtown Hopalong Cassidy trail of memorabilia, a mural and a statue, with an exhibit at the county tourist information center.

P.ad: Trailhead near Cambridge / Old Washington, Cambridge, OH 43725
P.w: A ~15-mile multi-use rail-trail for hiking, biking and horseback riding through forests and rolling countryside between Cambridge and Old Washington.

P.ad: Linden Ave at the Muskingum & Licking Rivers (US-40), Zanesville, OH 43701
P.w: A rare Y-shaped, three-way bridge at the confluence of the Licking and Muskingum Rivers — you can drive onto it and change direction mid-span. Carries US-40 (the National Road); the current span dates to 1902 and is famous enough that pilots recognize it from the air.

A ~10,000-acre wildlife conservation center on reclaimed strip-mine land, run by the Columbus Zoo — rhinos, giraffes, cheetahs and 25+ rare/endangered species roaming in mixed-species pastures. Open-air safaris, zipline, horseback and fishing tours. Seasonal (open daily May-Sept, weekends Oct); reservations required.

An Ohio History Connection museum with three galleries: the National Road (America's first federally funded highway), Western novelist Zane Grey (a Zanesville native descended from National Road builder Ebenezer Zane), and Ohio art pottery.

P.ad: 72 W Main St, New Concord, OH 43762
P.w: The boyhood home of astronaut and senator John Glenn — the first American to orbit Earth — presented as a costumed living-history tour of 1930s New Concord. Part of the Ohio History Connection system.

A NARM-affiliated art museum with American and European collections and, above all, 700+ examples of Zanesville-area art pottery — Weller, Roseville, Rookwood, J.B. Owens — celebrating the region's "Clay City" heritage.

The world's largest bronze-sculpture exhibition of any living sculptor — 300+ works in a 17,000 sq ft downtown studio/gallery where you can watch Cottrill (sculptor of Columbus's Brutus Buckeye) at work. Open Mon-Sat, suggested donation.

P.ad: Zane's Landing Park, N 5th St, Zanesville, OH 43701
P.w: A replica sternwheel riverboat offering sightseeing and dinner excursions on the Muskingum River from Zane's Landing Park at the west end of Market Street. Seasonal cruises.

P.ad: 7924 Cutler Lake Rd, Blue Rock, OH 43720
P.w: A quiet 322-acre state park around Cutler Lake, surrounded by 4,573 acres of Blue Rock State Forest, ~11 miles southeast of Zanesville — swimming, fishing, camping and hiking.

F.w: The original Wheeling home of Ohio Valley-style pizza: the DiCarlo brothers opened here in 1949 and the cold-cheese-on-hot-crust method became a regional icon.
A Centre Market institution since 1914 turning out 1,000+ fish sandwiches a day (2,500 on Fridays); called the country's best fish sandwich by Gourmet and featured on Food Network.

F.ad: 1035 Mount de Chantal Rd, Wheeling, WV 26003
F.w: A 2026 James Beard America's Classics winner; family-run since 1948 from Anna Figaretti's garage-made sauce, and previously named the best Italian restaurant in West Virginia.
Downtown gastropub from chef Matt Welsch — one of WV's inaugural Chef Ambassadors and a Food Network competition winner — serving locally sourced New American takes on Appalachian comfort food.
A cornerstone of Center Wheeling's revival since 2006, set in an 1860 building that won a $50,000 National Trust Backing Historic Small Restaurants grant; known for its wide crepe menu.
Chef Sarah Lydick's downtown bakery-cafe (opened 2018 in the former Lebanon Bakery) that won the Show of Hands pitch contest and quickly became one of Wheeling's most beloved spots.
Locally sourced American fare in the restored Waterfront Hall on the Wheeling riverfront, known for its burgers, fries and a menu that shifts with the seasons.
A longtime Wheeling neighborhood Italian spot whose 'world famous' GrecoRoni pepperoni rolls are a local tradition — Weelunk's pick in the best-pepperoni-roll conversation.

F.n: The Alpha Tavern (formerly Ye Olde Alpha)
F.w: The Edgwood site that was Ye Olde Alpha for nearly 90 years (est. 1932); after the old building came down it was rebuilt and revived by the Sparachanes as The Alpha Tavern in 2020.
Centre Market brewpub founded 2014 that helped resurrect Wheeling's brewing heritage and anchor downtown revival; now permanently closed but a notable chapter of the district's comeback.
A Washington, PA hot-dog lunch counter since the early 1930s, run by the Alexas family; its chili-topped 'everything' dog commands the kind of loyalty most brands only dream of.
Founded 1939 as the West Chestnut Spaghetti Inn by Palermo immigrants Angelo and Giacomina Passalacqua, it grew into Washington's most beloved Italian institution — 8+ decades and still family-run.

F.ad: 2175 E National Pike (US-40), Scenery Hill, PA 15360
F.w: Built 1794 as Hill's Tavern, the oldest continuously operating inn on the National Road; on the National Register, it sheltered Presidents Washington, Jackson and Polk and reopened after a 2015 fire.
Opened 1967 and named for the stonemasons and union workers who filled its tavern; a downtown Washington fixture for Italian-American cooking and an Observer-Reporter Best-of-the-Best regular.

Frank Sarris started making chocolate in his Canonsburg basement in 1960; the block-long factory store and Ice Cream Parlour is a Washington County landmark that draws visitors from across the region.

F.ad: 51800 National Rd E, St. Clairsville, OH 43950
F.w: A fourth-generation Ohio Valley staple on the National Road since 1961, serving Mary Mehlman's scratch-made favorites; WTRF and others have called it among the best cafeterias in Ohio.
The St. Clairsville outpost of the Undo's family (original in Benwood, WV, since 1953), a Belmont County local favorite for Italian cooking with a valley view and a sports bar.
An 85-year Bellaire hot-dog institution now in its fourth Gulla generation, built on a great-grandmother's Sicilian chili-sauce recipe brought over from the old country.
Downtown Cambridge on the National Road since 1931 (as Coney Island Lunch), family-run by the Theodosopoulos family since 1963; its coney dogs have been a mainstay for over 90 years.
A from-scratch Cambridge bakery running on the same family recipes since 1925; its Chinese tea cookies are so beloved that fans have them shipped as far as Germany.
A Zanesville institution since 1948, named after a customer who demanded his sundae be served in a soup bowl; a USA Today-recognized ice-cream stop known for its Tin Roof sundaes.
On Zanesville's Maple Avenue since 1958 and still family-run; Pizza Today has ranked it among the top 100 independently owned pizzerias in the nation.
The first brewery to operate in Zanesville since Prohibition (opened 2007 by Jay and Lori Wince) in a riverside brick building; an Ohio Magazine-featured craft brewpub known for its imperial stout.
A downtown Zanesville steak-and-Italian mainstay for 51 years; it closed in May 2025 and the Market Street space is being reborn under new ownership as the upscale Market Street Prime.
